paras: Renata Prado leads a team of eleven people in Sao Paulo. Her routine almost never changes, and she says that is the only reason it works. She wakes up at half past five, before anybody else in the house, and the first thing she does is take the dog to the small square at the end of the street. They are always the first ones there.

At half past six she wakes her son. He is fifteen, and he takes forty minutes to get ready for something that takes four minutes. She does not shout, and she does not help him look for his shoes. She learned that lesson two years ago. She makes coffee, she reads three messages, and she waits.

Her workday is full of meetings. She usually has four, and sometimes five, and she handles the difficult ones herself. She never eats at her desk. Her lunch break is one hour and she takes all of it, in a small restaurant two streets away, with her phone face down on the table. Her team knows that between one and two, she does not answer.

She gets home at seven. On a weekday she does not go out. She cooks something slow, she watches one episode of something, and she is in bed by eleven. She only really relaxes on the weekend, and everybody in that house knows it.
reading.source: A portrait written for this lesson, from a real routine in Sao Paulo.

choices: To explain how to become a team leader in a big company.
To show one busy woman's normal day, and the small rules she never breaks.
To argue that teenagers should get ready faster in the morning.

items.situation: Say what Renata does first in the morning, in one sentence, using she.
tips: She takes the dog to the square at half past five.
Watch the -s: she take is the mistake, she takes is the form.

items.situation: Now say two things she does NOT do.
tips: She does not shout, and she does not eat at her desk.
After does not, the verb loses the -s: not she does not eats.

items.situation: Ask a question about her son, using the third person.
tips: Not: Does he gets. The -s goes to does, never to both.

items.situation: The text says she never eats at her desk. Where exactly does never go?
tips: Before the verb: she never eats.
But after am, is and are: she is never late.

items.situation: Now say the same kind of sentence about your own son, and about your dog.
tips: My son wakes up at half past seven and he never gets ready on time.
My dog wakes me up before the alarm, and she waits at the door.

items.situation: Ask me two questions about my week: one with does, and one with a question word.
tips: Does your week look like hers?
What time do you usually get home?

listenings.text: My sister and I live in the same building, and our days could not be more different. She wakes up at five. Five. Nobody asks her to; she just does. She runs for forty minutes, she takes a cold shower, and by seven she has already answered every message she owes anybody. She never leaves the house without breakfast. I usually leave without my shoes on properly. She works from an office and she goes to about six meetings a day, and she says she likes them, which I do not understand at all. She does not check her phone after nine at night. She does not watch television. She reads. On Saturday she cleans the whole apartment before I am even awake, and then she asks me what I did all week. My routine is simpler. I wake up late, I work from home, I forget lunch, and I go to bed at two in the morning. We get on very well. We just never see each other before noon.

People think a routine makes your life smaller. In my experience it does the opposite. A routine is a set of decisions you make once, so that you do not have to make them again every morning while you are still half asleep. My neighbor gets up at the same time every single day, including Sunday. She walks her dog on the same street, she buys bread at the same place, and the man there starts making her coffee when he sees her cross the road. It sounds boring. It is not. Everything else in her week is chaos, and those forty minutes are the part nobody can move. So look at your own week and find the part that never changes. If there is nothing, that is the problem. Not the meetings, not the hours, not the traffic. The problem is that there is no hour in your week that belongs to you and always happens.
